catalog_quote: [p.115] 3. The phonological word. A word is characterized by the pauses which may precede and follow a string of phonemes. A pause may not be introduced within a word, however. Stress, on the other hand, is not a feature of words in the Konzime language. Phonological words may consist of one or of many syllables. ... [p.119] Syllabicity is one of the phonological "primes", rather difficult to define. In a tonal language such as Konzime, the nucleus of a syllable carries a contrastive tone and is thereby identifiable. The schewa which occurs between consonants which meet across syllable boundaries is not capable of bearing a contrastive tone ... [p.125] Of the 2.500 words I have recorded, all but approximately 46 have bitonal stems. The exceptions include 6 words having monotonal stems and approximately 40 words having tritonal stems. Since all stems are either monosyllabic or disyllabic…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim on the Persee page image we hold of Beavon 1983 p.115 (viewed) and in the held publisher scanned; the p.119 and p.125 supporting segments are also present. (2) The classification rests on the language's only published phonology (Beavon 1983, Africana Linguistica, 28 pp.), written by the principal describer, which states outright that stress is not a feature of Konzime words and analyses all prosody as H/L tone plus sentence intonation. Glottolog has no reference grammar for koon1245; its other 'phonology' entries are the 1977 unpublished precursor ms, a mis-tagged discourse study, and a mis-attached Gwa paper. SIL's archive (the Internet Archive listing, 39 items) adds only Beavon 1984 'Tone and intonation in Konzime' (15 pp., print-only). downloaded now: Beavon 1991 (verbal system; two-tone analysis, silent on stress, consistent) and a truncated Cheucle 2014

sources.quote: 'There is a simple two-tone distinction in Koozime, and there is also a small set of morphemes with toneless vowels.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere in pp.1-14; prosody handled entirely as H/L tone plus floating/replacive tonal morphemes. Describes Upriver Bajwe'e subdialect (1983 article describes Lomie/Nzime).
